title: How do we draw onion prices as one graph?
description: The monthly onion prices of two towns are drawn as one double column graph with one unit for ten rupees. The video finds the months when the second town is costlier and the gap in September. Keeko thinks a bar of five point nine units means five point nine rupees.
teaching_notes: One idea: a bar's height is the price divided by the scale, so the scale must be read before a price is read back. Watch for students who read the height in units as the price.

source: Draw the onion prices of the two towns as one double column graph with 1 unit = 10 rupees; the months the second town is costlier and the gap in September
video_script.why: The child has seen the two tables and now turns them into bars with a scale.
video_script.substitution: The book's own table of monthly onion prices in Yahapur and Wahapur.
video_script.anchor: Onion prices in rupees per kg, January to December. Yahapur: 25, 24, 26, 28, 30, 35, 39, 43, 49, 56, 59, 44. Wahapur: 19, 17, 23, 30, 38, 35, 42, 39, 53, 60, 52, 42.
video_script.wrong_answer: the price is five point nine rupees
video_script.wrong_move: Reads the bar's height in units as the price itself, forgetting that each unit stands for ten rupees.
video_script.payoff_line: Wahapur is costlier in five months, and in September by four rupees per kilogram.

final_answer.value: Wahapur costlier in 5 months (April, May, July, September, October); in September by 4 rupees per kg
final_answer.spoken: five months, and in September four rupees per kilogram

maths_rules: scale: 1 unit = 10 rupees, so height = price / 10
Wahapur higher: April 30 > 28, May 38 > 30, July 42 > 39, September 53 > 49, October 60 > 56 (5 months)
Yahapur higher in the other 6 months: January, February, March, August, November, December
video_script.design: One idea: the scale turns a price into a height. The two price rows sit in the anchor; on the board each price becomes a bar, side by side for each month, and the taller bar shows the costlier town.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book about onion prices in two towns.

<bookmark mark='m3'/>We will draw both towns in one graph, and ask in which months Wahapur is costlier.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Which town do you think is costlier in more months?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Each month gets two bars, side by side, one colour for each town.

beats.on_screen: height = price ÷ 10; Yahapur 59 → 59 ÷ 10 = 5.9 units; Wahapur 60 → 6 units

<bookmark mark='m2'/>Yahapur's fifty nine rupees makes a bar five point nine units tall.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Wahapur's sixty rupees makes a bar six units tall.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Wahapur is costlier in five months, and in September by four rupees per kilogram.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Those five months are April, May, July, September and October.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the bar is five point nine units tall, so the price is five point nine rupees.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But one unit stands for ten rupees, not for one rupee.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Five point nine units means fifty nine rupees.
